title: Chapter XIV

teacherSummary.text: The creature learns the De Laceys' history: Felix helped Safie's father, a Turkish merchant, escape unjust execution in Paris; the merchant betrayed them, and the family lost wealth and was exiled. Safie fled to find Felix.

vocabulary.definition: To make easy or less difficult
vocabulary.context: His plans were facilitated by the news which arrived from Paris.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “facilitate”: fac (Latin facere, "to make, do") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The generous nature of Safie was outraged by this command; she attempted to expostulate with her father, but he left her angrily, reiterating his tyrannical mandate.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reiterate”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To reason earnestly with a person on some impropriety of his conduct, representing the wrong he has done or intends,…
vocabulary.context: The generous nature of Safie was outraged by this command; she attempted to expostulate with her father, but he left her angrily, reiterating his tyrannical mandate.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “expostulate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Felix had procured passports in the name of his father, sister, and himself.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “passport”: port (Latin portare, "to carry"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: His blind and aged father, and his gentle sister, lay in a noisome dungeon, while he enjoyed the free air, and the society of her whom he loved.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “noisome”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: He was descended from a good family in France, where he had lived for many years in affluence, respected by his superiors, and beloved by his equals.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “affluence”: af- (Latin ad, "to") + flu (Latin fluere, "to flow") + -ence (Latin -entia, "state of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The generous nature of Safie was outraged by this command; she attempted to expostulate with her father, but he left her angrily, reiterating his tyrannical mandate.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mandate”: man (Latin manus, "hand") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To drive back or away, as with the foot
vocabulary.context: The young girl spoke in high and enthusiastic terms of her mother, who, born in freedom, spurned the bondage to which she was now reduced.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “spurn”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: “Felix had accidentally been present at the trial; his horror and indignation were uncontrollable, when he heard the decision of the court.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “uncontrollable”: un- (Old English un-, "not") + -able (Latin -abilis, "able to be"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To turn or roll round on, or as on, an axis, like a wheel
vocabulary.context: He revolved a thousand plans by which he should be enabled to prolong the deceit until it might be no longer necessary, and secretly to take his daughter with him when he departed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “revolve”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: The story reflects prejudices and politics of 18th-century France and attitudes toward the Ottoman world.

significance: Injustice repeats across the book; the virtuous suffer, and betrayal is common.
discussionQuestions: How does the De Laceys' story parallel the creature's own situation?
Where does plot appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the sublime power of nature?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XIV,” how does Shelley show injustice and exile? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XIV develops the idea of injustice and exile. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of plot and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses plot in Chapter XIV to complicate the reader's understanding of injustice and exile. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XIV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of injustice and exile responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XIV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of injustice and exile. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How does the De Laceys' story parallel the creature's own situation? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are facilitated, reiterating, expostulate, passports, noisome. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “His plans were facilitated by the news which arrived from Paris.” Webster's says: To make easy or less difficult. Now the word history: “facilitate”: fac (Latin facere, "to make, do") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. “reiterate”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “expostulate”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. The story reflects prejudices and politics of 18th-century France and attitudes toward the Ottoman world. Why does this chapter matter? Injustice repeats across the book; the virtuous suffer, and betrayal is common. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for plot.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see plot, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to injustice and exile.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Plot, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of plot. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

He was descended from a good family in France, where he had lived for many years in affluence, respected by his superiors, and beloved by his equals. segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Plot, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XIV,” how does Shelley show injustice and exile? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the plot you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about injustice and exile, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how plot shapes injustice and exile. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
